h1: How Do You Measure Whether a Workflow Change Helped?
seo_title: How to Measure Workflow Improvement: Time, Quality and Capacity | NATA
meta_description: Measure a workflow from a defined starting event to a defined outcome.

author.name: Fran Herrera
author.status: proposed byline; editorial approval not claimed

intent_evidence: Method article; exact search demand unmeasured
primary_question: How Do You Measure Whether a Workflow Change Helped?
section_questions: What should count as one workflow case?
What is the difference between handling time and elapsed time?
What should a workflow baseline record?
Why is average completion time not enough?
How do you check whether an improvement moved work elsewhere?
Are hours saved the same as financial savings?
How do you decide whether to keep a workflow change?
answer_capsule: Measure a workflow from a defined starting event to a defined outcome. Separate active work, waiting, clarification, and correction. Compare similar cases before and after the change, and record whether quality or effort moved elsewhere. A shorter completion time does not explain by itself what improved.
takeaways: Keep start, finish, and case types stable.
Separate handling time from elapsed time and waiting.
Report capacity, cost savings, and revenue effects accurately.

faqs.question: How many cases are enough to prove a workflow improved?
faqs.answer: There is no universal case count in this guide. State the sample, period, case mix, and limitations. A small trial can inform the next decision without supporting a claim about the entire business.

faqs.question: Can a time saving be attributed entirely to a new tool?
faqs.answer: Only if the evidence supports that attribution. Staffing, complexity, work volume, and other process changes may also affect results. Record those conditions rather than treating every before-and-after difference as the tool’s effect.

faqs.question: What should you do if speed improves but errors increase?
faqs.answer: Compare the change with the success and concern conditions agreed for the trial. Include correction effort and customer consequences. Faster handling alone is not sufficient evidence to keep the intervention.
